text: ISO 26262:  Test Specification for a functional requirement "HMI-Driver-Display shall be able to detect errors or unplausible data in the data stream and show a warning on Driver-Display". Write only a expected result
answer:
# ISO 26262 Test Specification – Expected Results

**Functional Requirement:** *HMI-Driver-Display shall be able to detect errors or implausible data in the data stream and show a warning on Driver-Display*

---

## Expected Results

### TC-001 | Detection of Corrupted Data in the Data Stream
> The Driver-Display **shall detect** the corrupted/invalid data within **≤ [X] ms** of occurrence and **shall not render** any incorrect or misleading information on the display.

---

### TC-002 | Display of Warning Message upon Error Detection
> Upon detection of an error or implausible data, the Driver-Display **shall present a clearly visible warning indicator/message** to the driver within **≤ [X] ms**, conforming to the defined warning presentation requirements (position, color, symbol, and priority level).

---

### TC-003 | Warning Persistence During Ongoing Error Condition
> The warning **shall remain continuously visible** on the Driver-Display for the entire duration of the error or implausible data condition, without flickering, disappearing, or being overridden by lower-priority display content.

---

### TC-004 | Warning Dismissal upon Recovery of Valid Data
> Once valid and plausible data is restored to the data stream, the warning **shall be cleared** from the Driver-Display within **≤ [X] ms**, and normal display operation **shall resume** without residual error indications.

---

### TC-005 | Handling of Missing / No Data (Signal Timeout)
> When no data is received within the defined timeout threshold **[X] ms**, the Driver-Display **shall detect the signal loss**, **shall not display** the last known (stale) value as current, and **shall activate** the corresponding warning on the display.

---

### TC-006 | Implausible Data Detection (Out-of-Range Values)
> When data values exceed the defined valid range **[Min – Max]**, the Driver-Display **shall identify** the data as implausible, **shall suppress** the implausible value from being shown, and **shall display** the warning to the driver.

---

### TC-007 | Simultaneous Multiple Error Conditions
> When multiple errors or implausible data conditions occur simultaneously, the Driver-Display **shall detect all active errors** and **shall display warnings** according to the defined priority scheme, ensuring **no warning is suppressed** without a documented priority rationale.

---

### TC-008 | Warning Display under Degraded System Conditions
> Under degraded system conditions (e.g., reduced voltage, high temperature), the Driver-Display **shall still detect** errors or implausible data and **shall correctly render** the warning without loss of visibility or functionality, meeting the ASIL-defined availability requirements.

---

### TC-009 | No False Warning (No Fault Injected)
> When valid and plausible data is continuously present in the data stream, the Driver-Display **shall not generate or display** any warning indication, confirming **no false-positive** warning behavior.

---

### TC-010 | Warning Reaction Time (Latency Verification)
> The end-to-end latency from error/implausible data occurrence in the data stream to the warning being **visually confirmed on the Driver-Display shall not exceed [X] ms**, as defined by the system timing requirement and ASIL decomposition.

---

**Note:** All expected results shall be verified against the applicable ASIL level, and evidence shall be traceable to the safety goal and functional safety requirement as per **ISO 26262-6**.

text: ISO 26262: Test Specification for the Technical Requirement "CAN Interface  shall ensure that all received signals are forwarded to their destination"? Write only test procedure!
answer:
# Test Specification: CAN Interface Signal Forwarding

## Test Procedure

---

### TP-CAN-FWD-001: Nominal Signal Forwarding – Single Signal

**Objective:** Verify that a single received CAN signal is correctly forwarded to its defined destination.

**Preconditions:**
- DUT is powered and initialized
- CAN bus is operational (no bus-off, no error-passive state)
- Test equipment (CANoe/CANalyzer or equivalent) connected to CAN bus
- Destination interface (memory, SW component, actuator interface) is accessible for readback

**Steps:**
1. Configure test tool to transmit a CAN message with a defined signal value (e.g., Signal_A = 0x55) on the configured CAN ID.
2. Trigger transmission of the CAN message on the bus.
3. Wait for the defined processing cycle (≤ defined forwarding latency).
4. Read back the signal value at the defined destination (e.g., internal RAM variable, RTE port, output CAN message).
5. Compare the received signal value at the destination with the transmitted value.

**Expected Result:**
- Signal value at destination equals transmitted value (0x55).
- No signal loss or corruption observed.
- Forwarding occurs within the specified latency.

---

### TP-CAN-FWD-002: Nominal Signal Forwarding – All Defined Signals (Full Coverage)

**Objective:** Verify that **all** signals defined in the CAN communication matrix (DBC/ARXML) are forwarded to their respective destinations.

**Preconditions:**
- Complete CAN database (DBC/ARXML) loaded into test tool
- All signal-to-destination mappings documented in the Signal Routing Table
- DUT is fully initialized

**Steps:**
1. Load the complete CAN signal routing table (source CAN ID + signal name → destination).
2. For each signal defined in the routing table:
   a. Transmit the CAN message containing the signal with a defined test value (e.g., minimum valid value).
   b. Wait for forwarding cycle to complete.
   c. Read back the value at the defined destination.
   d. Log result (PASS/FAIL) per signal.
3. Repeat Step 2 for maximum valid value for each signal.
4. Generate test report listing all signals with forwarding status.

**Expected Result:**
- 100% of signals defined in the routing table are forwarded to their correct destination.
- All read-back values match transmitted values.
- No signal is missing or routed to an incorrect destination.

---

### TP-CAN-FWD-003: Signal Forwarding Under Continuous Bus Load

**Objective:** Verify signal forwarding under high CAN bus load conditions.

**Preconditions:**
- CAN bus load generator configured to produce ≥ 80% bus load with background traffic
- DUT operational

**Steps:**
1. Start CAN bus load generator to simulate ≥ 80% bus load.
2. Transmit target CAN messages containing all signals under test at their nominal cycle time.
3. Monitor destination interfaces for all expected forwarded signal values over a period of 60 seconds.
4. Record any missed forwarding events, delayed forwarding, or corrupted values.
5. Stop bus load generator.
6. Evaluate results against specification (latency, completeness).

**Expected Result:**
- All signals are forwarded to destinations without loss.
- Forwarding latency does not exceed the specified maximum under high bus load.
- No signal corruption observed.

---

### TP-CAN-FWD-004: Signal Forwarding After CAN Bus Recovery (Bus-Off Recovery)

**Objective:** Verify that signal forwarding resumes correctly after CAN bus-off recovery.

**Preconditions:**
- DUT operational and forwarding signals nominally
- Capability to inject bus errors (e.g., CANstress or equivalent tool)

**Steps:**
1. Confirm all signals are being forwarded nominally (baseline check).
2. Inject CAN bus errors to force the DUT CAN controller into bus-off state.
3. Verify DUT enters bus-off state (monitor via diagnostic or status register).
4. Remove error injection and allow DUT to perform bus-off recovery (per ISO 11898).
5. After recovery confirmation, transmit all defined CAN messages with known signal values.
6. Read back all signal values at their defined destinations.
7. Compare read-back values with transmitted values.

**Expected Result:**
- DUT recovers from bus-off state within specified recovery time.
- All signals are correctly forwarded after recovery.
- No permanent loss of signal forwarding observed.

---

### TP-CAN-FWD-005: Signal Forwarding Integrity – Boundary Values

**Objective:** Verify that signals are forwarded correctly for boundary (minimum and maximum) raw values.

**Preconditions:**
- Signal value ranges defined in DBC/ARXML
- DUT operational

**Steps:**
1. For each signal under test:
   a. Transmit the signal with raw value = **minimum** valid value.
   b. Read back value at destination.
   c. Verify value matches.
   d. Transmit the signal with raw value = **maximum** valid value.
   e. Read back value at destination.
   f. Verify value matches.
   g. Transmit the signal with raw value = **0x00** (zero).
   h. Read back value at destination.
   i. Verify value matches.

**Expected Result:**
- All boundary values are forwarded without modification, truncation, or corruption.

---

### TP-CAN-FWD-006: Signal Forwarding Latency Measurement

**Objective:** Verify that signal forwarding latency is within the specified maximum latency.

**Preconditions:**
- Timestamp capability available on both CAN reception and destination readback
- Maximum forwarding latency specified (e.g., T_max = X ms)

**Steps:**
1. Configure test tool to timestamp the exact moment a CAN message is transmitted onto the bus (T_send).
2. Configure monitoring on the destination interface to timestamp the moment the forwarded signal value becomes available (T_arrive).
3. Transmit the CAN message with a known signal value.
4. Record T_send and T_arrive.
5. Calculate forwarding latency: **ΔT = T_arrive − T_send**.
6. Repeat 100 times per signal to capture statistical distribution (min, max, average).
7. Compare max observed ΔT against specified T_max.

**Expected Result:**
- Maximum forwarding latency ΔT ≤ T_max for all signals.
- No forwarding event exceeds the specified latency.

---

### TP-CAN-FWD-007: Signal Forwarding – Correct Destination Routing Verification

**Objective:** Verify that each signal is forwarded **only** to its correct destination and not to unintended destinations.

**Preconditions:**
- All destination interfaces are monitorable
- Signal routing table available

**Steps:**
1. For each signal under test:
   a. Transmit the CAN message containing the signal with a unique identifiable test pattern value.
   b. Monitor **all** possible destinations simultaneously.
   c. Verify that the signal value appears **only** at the defined correct destination.
   d. Verify that the signal value does **not** appear at any unintended destination.
2. Log results per signal.

**Expected Result:**
- Each signal is routed exclusively to its specified destination.
- No cross-routing or unintended signal forwarding is observed.

---

### TP-CAN-FWD-008: Signal Forwarding During DUT Initialization Phase

**Objective:** Verify behavior of signal forwarding during DUT startup/initialization.

**Preconditions:**
- DUT startup sequence is observable
- CAN messages transmittable during DUT initialization

**Steps:**
1. Start transmitting defined CAN messages with known signal values **before** DUT power-on.
2. Power on DUT and start initialization sequence.
3. Monitor destinations for forwarded signal values throughout the initialization phase.
4. Record the first moment forwarded signals become available at destinations.
5. Verify that once initialization is complete, all signals are correctly forwarded.
6. Verify no incorrect or corrupted signal values are forwarded during initialization.

**Expected Result:**
- After DUT initialization is complete, all signals are correctly forwarded.
- No safety-critical incorrect values are forwarded during initialization.
- Behavior during initialization is consistent with the specification.

---

## Pass/Fail Criteria Summary

| Test Case | Pass Criterion |
|-----------|---------------|
| TP-CAN-FWD-001 | Signal value at destination equals transmitted value |
| TP-CAN-FWD-002 | 100% of all signals forwarded to correct destination |
| TP-CAN-FWD-003 | No signal loss or violation of latency under ≥80% bus load |
| TP-CAN-FWD-004 | Full forwarding restored after bus-off recovery |
| TP-CAN-FWD-005 | All boundary values forwarded without corruption |
| TP-CAN-FWD-006 | Max latency ΔT ≤ T_max for all signals |
| TP-CAN-FWD-007 | No cross-routing; correct destination only |

answer:
# Paper Cranes and Ink Stains

### A Novel

---

## Part One: The Man Who Had Everything

---

### Chapter One: The Showroom Floor

The morning light came through the floor-to-ceiling windows of Miyamoto Stationery Corporation's Tokyo headquarters in long, golden sheets, pooling on the polished concrete floor like something precious that had been spilled and no one had bothered to clean up. It landed on the rows of sample displays — fountain pens in their velvet cradles, leather-bound notebooks fanned open to show their ivory pages, washi paper pressed into sheets so fine you could almost see through them — and turned the entire showroom into something that resembled a museum more than an office.

Kato Haruki arrived at eight forty-five, fifteen minutes before the rest of the sales team, as he always did.

He came through the glass doors with his coat folded over one arm, his briefcase in the other hand, his dark hair slightly damp from where he had walked two blocks from Shinjuku Station in the early October drizzle. He was thirty-one years old. He was, by any reasonable measure, the most beautiful person who worked on the fourth floor of Miyamoto Stationery Corporation — and this was a floor that employed forty-three people, several of whom were considered quite attractive by general consensus.

It was not simply that his features were symmetrical, though they were. It was not simply that he was tall, or that his suits always fit as though they had been designed specifically for his body, or that his hands — which he used with great expressiveness when he was making a pitch — were the kind of hands that made female clients unconsciously lean forward across the conference table. It was something in the way he carried himself. An ease. A warmth that was entirely natural, not performed, which made it somehow more devastating than if it had been.

Haruki set his briefcase on his desk, draped his coat over the back of his chair, and turned on his computer. He looked at the rain against the window for a moment with the same equanimity he brought to everything, then sat down and opened his email.

There were fourteen new messages. Three were from clients. One was from the head of the corporate accounts division, a man named Yamaguchi Tetsuya, who was sixty-two years old and had been at Miyamoto for thirty years and who considered Haruki to be the most promising sales representative the company had produced in the last decade, a fact he expressed through a combination of mentorship and barely concealed pride, as though Haruki were a particularly successful orchid he had cultivated. One was from a client in Osaka who wanted to expand her order. One was the company newsletter.

Haruki read them in order, responding where necessary, and was halfway through his third reply when the door opened and the rest of the team began to arrive.

He heard them before he saw them — the particular sound of a group of people whose day had not yet started in earnest, the shuffling of coats and umbrellas, the small complaints about the rain and the train delays, the beeping of the coffee machine in the break room down the hall. He did not look up from his screen. He had learned, over the years, that looking up when people entered a room had a way of creating interactions he didn't always have the energy for before nine in the morning.

"Kato-san."

He looked up.

Fujimoto Rie was standing at the edge of his desk. She was twenty-seven, with short hair and very direct eyes, and she worked in marketing on the same floor. She was holding two cups of coffee.

"I got you one," she said, setting it on the corner of his desk with the careful deliberateness of someone making an offering.

"Thank you," Haruki said, and smiled at her.

Fujimoto Rie's cheeks went slightly pink. This happened often. Haruki had long since learned to notice it without reacting to it, the way one learns not to react to a car alarm in a neighborhood where car alarms are common.

"Big day today?" she asked, making no immediate move to return to her own desk.

"Presentation at eleven for Nakashima Publishing. Then follow-up calls in the afternoon."

"You'll be wonderful," she said, with a conviction that suggested she had never doubted it.

"Thank you, Fujimoto-san."

She went back to her desk. Haruki returned to his email.

---

From the cluster of desks near the window on the north side of the floor, Mishima Daisuke watched this exchange with the flat, settled feeling of someone who has watched the same movie too many times and has stopped finding it entertaining.

Mishima was thirty-four, three years older than Haruki, and he had joined Miyamoto Stationery Corporation two years before Haruki had. He was not unattractive — he had been told this, usually by relatives at family gatherings, with the specific enthusiasm people reserve for compliments they are not entirely sure of — and he was, by any objective standard, a competent sales representative. His numbers were solid. His client retention rate was good. He had won the quarterly award twice.

Haruki won it every quarter.

Not through any aggression or maneuvering. Not through politics or favoritism, though Mishima had spent considerable mental energy exploring those possibilities. Simply by being better. Simply by being the kind of person who walked into a room and made everyone in it want to give him what he was asking for, not because they felt pressured but because it genuinely felt like the right thing to do.

It was, Mishima had decided, deeply unfair.

"Look at him," he muttered.

Okabe Shiro, who sat at the desk next to his and who was twenty-nine and nursing a grudge about a promotion that had gone to someone else, looked up from his screen. "Fujimoto again?"

"Fujimoto, Tanaka from accounting, that new client from last month — the one from the paper mill—"

"Suzuki-san."

"Suzuki-san. He didn't even do anything. He just *smiled* at her during the site visit and now she's placed the largest single order the company has received this year."

Okabe made a sound that was somewhere between agreement and resignation. "Yamaguchi-san is going to give him the Tenmei account."

"I know."

"I heard it from Inoue in admin. It's already decided."

Mishima looked at Haruki across the office — at his dark head bent slightly toward his screen, at the easy line of his shoulders, at the small smile that appeared on his face as he read something, directed at no one, just a private moment of amusement that somehow managed to make him more attractive — and felt the familiar heat of something he preferred not to examine too closely settle in his chest.

"He's not even that good," Mishima said, without conviction.

Okabe said nothing. They both knew this was untrue.

---

### Chapter Two: The Administrative Floor

The third floor of Miyamoto Stationery Corporation was quieter than the fourth.

It was the floor where the administrative and clerical staff worked — the people who processed the orders that the sales team generated, who maintained the client databases, who handled the correspondence and the filing and the thousand small tasks that kept a company of three hundred employees running without anyone on the upper floors needing to think about it. The third floor smelled of printer ink and paper and the faint ghost of someone's lunch. The carpet was a different color from the fourth floor — a more subdued gray, chosen, presumably, for its practicality.

Nishimura Kenji had worked on the third floor for four years.

He was twenty-eight years old, and he sat at a desk near the back of the open-plan office, close enough to the window to see a sliver of gray sky but not so close that the light caused problems with his screen. His desk was the tidiest in the office — not aggressively so, not in the way that suggests someone is performing tidiness for an audience, but in the quiet way of a person for whom order is simply more comfortable than chaos. His pens were in a small ceramic cup. His papers were in labeled folders. There was a small succulent on the corner of his desk in a pot painted with a pattern of tiny blue triangles, which a coworker had given him as a birthday present two years ago and which he watered with precise regularity.

Kenji was, by any fair assessment, unremarkable in appearance. He was slightly below average height, with the kind of face that was pleasant and kind without being particularly memorable — soft eyes behind wire-rimmed glasses, a mouth that was prone to small, apologetic smiles, hair that was always slightly in need of a trim. He wore clothes that were neat but unassuming: dark trousers, plain shirts in muted colors, a cardigan in the colder months that his mother had given him and that he wore with complete unselfconsciousness despite the fact that cardigans were not, in the estimation of his coworkers, particularly fashionable.

He was the kind of person who became invisible in a large group, and who was, at some level, comfortable with this.

He was also the most reliable person on the third floor, a fact acknowledged by everyone who worked with him including his supervisor, Hayashi-san, who had written in his last performance review that Kenji was "indispensable to the smooth functioning of the department" and "possessed of a quiet diligence that more visibly ambitious employees would do well to emulate," which Kenji had read with a mixture of quiet pride and slight embarrassment, folded carefully, and placed in the bottom drawer of his desk.

"Nishimura-kun."

He looked up. Hayashi-san was standing at his desk with a stack of documents.

"The order confirmations for the Tenmei account need to be cross-referenced with the inventory records before end of day. Also, Yamamoto-san from accounts is asking for the quarterly reconciliation."

"I'll have them both done by three," Kenji said.

Hayashi-san nodded, set the documents on his desk, and walked away. Kenji looked at the documents for a moment, then opened the appropriate files on his computer and began.

This was, largely, what his days consisted of. Documents. Spreadsheets. Reconciliations. The occasional phone call from a client or a supplier, which he handled with careful politeness and a genuine desire to be helpful that tended to surprise people who expected bureaucratic indifference. He worked steadily and without complaint and took his lunch break at twelve-thirty, usually alone, usually eating a bento his mother had prepared — she still made him lunch, though he lived alone, because she came to visit every Sunday and made a week's worth, and he had long since stopped arguing about this — and reading a paperback novel with the focused pleasure of someone for whom reading is not a pastime but a necessity.

He did not go to many company events. Not because he was antisocial — he liked his coworkers, genuinely, and was always remembered fondly by people who had worked with him — but because large social gatherings required a kind of performance he found exhausting, the constant management of impression, the navigation of group dynamics, the noise and the standing and the small talk that felt like work of a different and less satisfying kind.

He had been at Miyamoto Stationery Corporation for four years and had met the sales team on the fourth floor perhaps a dozen times, mostly in the elevator or in the lobby or at the two company-wide parties held each year, which he attended dutifully and left at a reasonable hour.

He knew Kato Haruki by reputation — everyone on the third floor did. The sales team's results filtered down eventually, became office conversation, became part of the mythology of the company. Kato Haruki, who had joined five years ago and had become the top sales representative in three. Who had, according to Matsuda from client services who sometimes worked with the sales team on complex accounts, a gift for making people feel understood that was almost alarming. Who was, according to essentially everyone who mentioned him, extremely good-looking, which Kenji registered as information the way one registers the weather — as a fact about the world that did not particularly affect him.

He had spoken to Kato Haruki once, in the elevator, in his second year at the company. Haruki had held the door for him, and Kenji had thanked him, and Haruki had smiled and asked him which floor, and Kenji had said three, and Haruki had pressed the button and that had been the end of it.

He had not thought about it since.

---

### Chapter Three: The Best in the Business

The Nakashima Publishing presentation went the way Haruki's presentations usually went.

He arrived ten minutes early, set up the samples he had brought — a selection of premium notebooks, fountain pens, and custom washi stationery that Miyamoto had developed specifically for publishing houses who understood the value of quality materials — and arranged them on the conference table with the care of someone who knew that the physical beauty of the products was itself part of the argument.

When the Nakashima team arrived — four people, the director of operations, her assistant, the head of design, and a younger man whose exact role Haruki had not yet determined — he greeted them with the warm, unhurried attention that was, Yamaguchi-san had once told him, his greatest professional asset. Not charm, exactly. Charm implied a kind of artificiality, a gap between the performed warmth and the actual feeling. With Haruki, there was no gap. He was simply genuinely interested in people.

He listened to what the director of operations said about their current supplier and what was missing. He asked questions that suggested he had considered the matter seriously before the meeting, which he had. He showed them the samples not as products to be sold but as solutions to specific problems they had articulated, which meant that when he finally got to the pricing, it felt like a conclusion rather than a sales pitch.

The director of operations, a woman in her fifties named Ogawa-san who had been in the publishing industry for thirty years and who had, Haruki suspected, a finely calibrated instinct for anyone trying to manipulate her, looked at him across the table with an expression he had learned to recognize.

"You're not like the last sales representative we dealt with," she said.

"I'll take that as a compliment," Haruki said.

She laughed. "You should." She looked at the samples again. "We'll start with the notebook line. The full range. And I want to discuss the custom imprinting options."

After the meeting — which ran twenty minutes over schedule because Ogawa-san had more questions than expected, all of them good ones — Haruki packed up the samples that were going back to the office and left the ones they had decided on as reference copies. He shook hands with everyone. In the elevator going down, he allowed himself a moment of quiet satisfaction — not triumphalism, which he found distasteful, but a simple acknowledgment that things had gone well.

His phone buzzed. A message from Yamaguchi-san:

*How did it go?*

Haruki typed back: *Well. They're starting with the full notebook line.*

Three dots appeared immediately. Then: *Excellent. Come see me when you're back. I want to talk to you about the Tenmei party.*

Haruki looked at this for a moment. He had heard about the Tenmei party — everyone on the fourth floor had. Tenmei Enterprises was one of Miyamoto's largest corporate clients, a conglomerate that used Miyamoto's premium stationery products across all of its divisions, which meant a purchasing relationship worth several million yen annually. The president of Tenmei, Haruki knew, was a woman named Toda Sakura who had inherited the company from her father eight years ago and had, by all accounts, substantially grown it.

The annual Tenmei party was a significant event on Miyamoto's social calendar. Being invited was considered an indicator of standing.

He put his phone in his pocket and stepped out into the October afternoon.

---

When he got back to the office, Yamaguchi-san was waiting for him with the particular air of a man who has been looking forward to a conversation.

Yamaguchi Tetsuya was sixty-two years old and looked like what he was — a man who had spent four decades in business, who had the permanent slight tan of someone who played golf on weekends, whose suits were good but slightly out of fashion in a way that suggested he no longer paid attention to fashion and was entirely at peace with this. He had a face that had been handsome once and was now interesting, with deep lines around his eyes and mouth that suggested he had smiled and frowned in roughly equal measure throughout his life.

He liked Haruki with the uncomplicated affection of a mentor who has found an ideal student. He also, in some way he would not have been able to articulate, understood that Haruki's success was partly a reflection of his own judgment in recognizing and cultivating him. This was not cynical. It was simply true.

"Sit down," he said.

Haruki sat.

"The Tenmei party is the twenty-second. Friday evening. Toda-san's company is celebrating fifteen years of their corporate division."

"I heard about it," Haruki said.

"I'm taking you. And I want to bring someone from the third floor — Nishimura, the clerk who handles the Tenmei account documentation. Toda-san asked specifically for someone who could answer detailed questions about order history if needed."

"Nishimura-san," Haruki said, placing the name. He thought of the elevator, four years ago. The polite exchange. The slightly rumpled cardigan. "Yes, I know who he is."

"He's a good kid," Yamaguchi said, with the slightly patronizing warmth he used when discussing anyone younger than forty-five. "Reliable. Quiet. Won't cause any trouble." He said this as though it were the highest possible praise for a person attending a client party, which in Yamaguchi's professional philosophy it essentially was.

"When should I tell him?"

"I'll let Hayashi-san know on the third floor. You don't need to do anything except show up and be yourself." Yamaguchi leaned back in his chair, looking at Haruki with the slightly satisfied expression of someone who knows they are placing their best piece on the board. "Toda-san will appreciate meeting you in person. She's heard about you."

"Has she," Haruki said, with the flatness of someone who has heard variations of this sentence many times.

"She specifically asked if the sales representative handling her account would be attending." Yamaguchi's expression shifted very slightly — a flicker of something that might have been a warning, quickly suppressed. "She's an interesting woman. Accomplished. Formidable."

"I'll be on my best behavior," Haruki said.

Yamaguchi looked at him for a moment. "Yes," he said. "Do that."

---

## Part Two: The Party

---

### Chapter Four: Getting Ready

On the morning of October twenty-second, Kenji arrived at work to find a note on his desk from Hayashi-san reminding him that he was to leave the office at six o'clock for the Tenmei party and that he should bring the account documentation folder Hayashi-san had prepared for him.

Kenji looked at this note for some time.

He had been informed about the party four days ago, summoned to Hayashi-san's office and told, in Hayashi-san's brisk and efficient way, that he was representing the department at an important client event, that he should dress appropriately, that he was to answer any questions about the Tenmei account clearly and accurately, and that he was not to worry because Yamaguchi-san from the sales division would be there to manage the social dimensions of the evening.

Kenji had said, "Yes, of course," and gone back to his desk and spent the rest of that afternoon in a state of low-grade anxiety that he had managed, over four days, to suppress to the level of a persistent background hum.

He did not enjoy client parties. He was aware of this and considered it a personal failing of some kind, the way one considers shyness a failing — not a moral one, but a practical one, a limitation that cost you things. He was perfectly competent at his work. He was perfectly capable of explaining order histories and account documentation to anyone who asked. He was simply not good at the performance of ease that parties required, the effortless social motion from one conversation to another, the projection of warmth and accessibility that seemed to come naturally to some people and that he had to consciously construct, brick by brick, for every interaction.

He would manage. He always did.

At lunch, his phone showed a message from his mother asking how he was, and he wrote back that he was fine, that there was a work party tonight, that he would call her over the weekend. She sent back a string of emoji that he had learned, through years of patient observation, to decode: a flower, a sparkle, a small smiling face. This meant she was proud of him. He put his phone in his pocket and returned to the Tenmei reconciliation.

At five-thirty, he went to the bathroom and assessed himself in the mirror with the pragmatic unsenti­mentality he brought to most things. He had worn his best suit — dark navy, which his mother had bought him two years ago for his cousin's wedding and which still fit — and a white shirt and a plain dark tie. He had combed his hair. His glasses were clean. He looked, he thought, presentable. Not remarkable. Presentable.

He picked up the documentation folder, put on his coat, and went to the lobby to meet Yamaguchi-san.

---

Haruki was already there when he arrived, standing near the glass doors with his coat on, scrolling through something on his phone. He looked up when Kenji came off the elevator.

For a moment Kenji had the slightly unreal sensation that sometimes strikes people who encounter in person someone they have only known by reputation. Kato Haruki was taller than he remembered from the elevator encounter four years ago — or perhaps Kenji had simply not retained the information properly. He was also, undeniably, more striking than his reputation had suggested, though Kenji had always assumed some degree of exaggeration in the way people talked about him. There seemed to be no exaggeration. He was simply — and Kenji registered this with the same mild neutrality with which he registered all aesthetic facts — extremely good-looking. Dark eyes, strong jaw, the kind of effortless elegance in his posture that suggested he was not trying.

He was also smiling, which helped, because it shifted the effect from intimidating to simply pleasant.

"Nishimura-san," Haruki said, with the ease of someone who has never been uncomfortable introducing himself. "Kato Haruki. Sales team."

"Yes, I know," Kenji said, and then felt slightly awkward about this, as though knowing who someone was before meeting them was a mild violation. "I mean — we've met briefly before. A few years ago. In the elevator."

Haruki looked at him with what seemed like genuine interest. "Did we? I'm sorry, I don't—"

"No, you wouldn't remember. It was just a moment." Kenji adjusted his grip on the documentation folder. "It's nice to meet you properly."

"You too," Haruki said, and it had the quality of something he meant, which Kenji noticed without knowing exactly what to do with.

Yamaguchi-san arrived three minutes later, slightly breathless and apologizing for the delay in the way of someone who is never actually late but treats two minutes as a serious infraction. He looked at both of them with the brisk approval of a general inspecting his troops.

"Good. You look presentable, both of you. Nishimura, you have the documentation?"

"Yes, Yamaguchi-san."

"Good boy." He turned to the door. "The car is outside. Let's go."

---

### Chapter Five: Toda Sakura

The Tenmei party was held on the top floor of a hotel in Akasaka, in a private event space that looked out over the city in a way that was clearly designed to remind everyone in the room of the scale of what they were celebrating.

Kenji stood near the window for the first twenty minutes and tried not to look overwhelmed.

The room was full of people who were comfortable in rooms like this, which was its own particular kind of social pressure. Men and women in expensive clothes, speaking with the fluency of people who had attended many parties and had long since stopped needing to think about how. There were canapés on silver trays. There was champagne that arrived at your elbow before you had quite decided you wanted it. There was a low current of conversation and music and laughter that felt, to Kenji, like weather — something you were inside of rather than something you were participating in.

He had answered two questions about the account documentation from a Tenmei finance director who had approached him specifically, recognized him from the folder he was still holding — he really needed to put it down somewhere — and seemed reassured by his answers. He had eaten two pieces of something on bread that he thought might be salmon. He had accepted a glass of champagne and was holding it with the cautious awareness of someone who does not drink often and would like to remain that way.

Haruki, he noticed, was doing what Haruki presumably always did at parties of this kind. He was speaking to people with the same easy attention he had demonstrated in the lobby — truly listening, it seemed, genuinely present in each conversation, moving from one group to another without the social awkwardness that transitions usually required. Yamaguchi-san hovered nearby with the proprietary pride of a man who has produced something excellent and wants to be standing close to it when others notice.

Kenji watched him for a moment — just a moment, with the idle curiosity one brings to watching any person who is clearly exceptional at something — and then looked back at the window and the lights of the city below.

"You're the one from the documentation department."

He turned. A woman was standing beside him.

She was, at a guess, forty-five. She was extremely well-dressed — a midnight blue suit with a quality that suggested it had been made specifically for her — with dark hair cut in a precise, geometric style and the kind of face that had been beautiful when she was younger and had become, with age, something more interesting than beautiful. She had dark eyes that were very direct, and the general bearing of someone who was accustomed to the complete attention of every room she entered.

Kenji recognized her from the company photographs he had seen in the account files. Toda Sakura. President of Tenmei Enterprises.

He straightened involuntarily. "Nishimura Kenji, from the administrative division. I handle the documentation for the Tenmei account."

"I know," she said. "I asked who was coming." She looked at him with a slightly amused assessment that he found difficult to interpret. "You're very organized. The account records are the best-maintained of any of our suppliers."

"Thank you," Kenji said, genuinely pleased by this, because it was the kind of compliment that mattered to him.

She looked past him, and her expression changed.

It was a subtle shift — the way light changes when a cloud passes over it, there and then not there. She was looking at something across the room, and her eyes had taken on a quality of sharp, concentrated interest.

Kenji followed her gaze.

She was looking at Haruki.

---

Toda Sakura had, in forty-five years of life, met a great many men. She had been in business for twenty years, which meant she had operated in environments where appearance and charisma and intelligence were all currency, and she had developed a fine-grained appreciation for these qualities in others. She had also been told, by various people over the years, that she had a tendency toward imperiousness, a preference for getting what she wanted that had been tolerated — even admired — in the context of business and that had served her less well in personal life.

She was not currently in a relationship. She had not been for two years, since a parting that had been more acrimonious than she liked to remember. She was not, generally, the kind of person who saw a man at a party and felt anything she would describe as wanting. She was too self-possessed for that, too careful with what she revealed even to herself.

But when Yamaguchi-san brought Kato Haruki to meet her — when Haruki smiled and shook her hand and looked at her with the full, warm attention that was apparently his default mode — she felt something shift in the room, the way the air changes before a storm, and she decided, with the swift decision-making that had built her company, that she intended to know him better.

"Kato-san," she said. "I've heard so much about you."

"All good, I hope," Haruki said, with a small, slightly self-deprecating smile that suggested he was mildly bored by compliments without being rude about it.

She liked this. She liked most things about him, assessed in these first minutes: the intelligence behind the warmth, the way he was present without being deferential, the easy assurance that never tipped into arrogance. She found herself leaning slightly forward, which she noticed and chose not to correct.

"Walk with me," she said. "I want to show you something."

She took him to the far side of the room, near the window, ostensibly to show him a commissioned artwork on the wall that depicted the history of the company. She asked him about his approach to the account, listened to his answers, moved gradually from the professional to the personal in the way of someone who knows how these transitions work.

Haruki was gracious. He was attentive. He was everything his reputation had suggested.

He also maintained, with extraordinary skill, a distance that felt friendly rather than cold — a warmth that did not encourage the specific kind of closeness she was angling toward. She was experienced enough to recognize this and experienced enough to find it interesting rather than discouraging.

When she placed her hand on his arm — lightly, casually, the kind of touch that is always deniable — he did not remove it immediately. But he shifted, very slightly, so that the angle of his body redirected the conversation without making a scene of the redirection, and said something about a product line he thought would be ideal for Tenmei's executive correspondence, and somehow they were discussing fountain pens and she was still facing him but the particular charged quality of the moment had been gracefully dismantled.

*Interesting,* she thought.

She tried again, later in the evening, with more directness. Less patience.

"I'm having a dinner next month," she said. "Small gathering. I'd like you to come. Personally."

The emphasis was clear.

Haruki met her eyes. His expression was kind — genuinely kind, which was, she thought, more irritating than simple refusal would have been.

"Toda-san," he said, quietly, so that only she could hear. "I'm honored. But I have to be honest with you, because I think you deserve honesty and because I think this relationship is important, professionally — I don't think that would be appropriate."

The room went very slightly cold.

"Appropriate," she repeated.

"It's a privilege to work with your company," he said, and the warmth was entirely real, which somehow made it worse. "I want to maintain that."

There was a moment — very brief, but visible, at least to Kenji who happened to be watching from across the room, his champagne glass forgotten in his hand — in which Toda Sakura's face rearranged itself from desire to something considerably colder.

"Of course," she said. Her smile was the smile she wore in board meetings when someone had said something she was going to address later. "You're very professional, Kato-san."

She turned and walked back to the center of the room.

Yamaguchi-san, who had been monitoring the situation from a careful distance in the way of an experienced corporate soldier who knows when something is going wrong but hopes he is mistaken, approached Haruki with an expression caught precisely between anxiety and the need to not show anxiety.

"Everything all right?" he said, which was the least revealing version of the many more urgent questions he wanted to ask.

"Fine," Haruki said. His voice was level. "I think I'll get some water."

Kenji, still standing near the window, watched him cross the room. Haruki's posture was as easy as it had been all evening — the kind of carriage that doesn't break under pressure — but there was something around his eyes, a tightness, that suggested the ease was now being maintained rather than simply existing.

He thought: *That must have been difficult.*

Then he thought: *I should probably put this documentation folder somewhere.*

### Chapter Six: After

The car back to the office was quiet.

Yamaguchi-san spoke on his phone for most of the journey, his voice carefully neutral, speaking to someone Kenji suspected was higher in the company than Yamaguchi himself. The conversation was brief and concerned the party in the oblique way of people who know they are being overheard.

When it ended, Yamaguchi-san was quiet for a moment, looking out the window at the city moving past. Then he said, without turning around: "She called while we were in the car."

Neither Haruki nor Kenji said anything.

"She expressed—" Yamaguchi paused, choosing the word. "Disappointment. With how the evening went."

Haruki looked at his hands. "I'm sorry," he said. "I handled it the best way I could."

"I know you did." Yamaguchi's voice was not angry. It was tired, which was somehow worse. "I know. But she's a significant account, Kato."

The car moved through the lit streets. The rain had come back, and the window was streaked with it, the lights of the city smeared and softened.

"I'll fix it," Haruki said. "I'll call her assistant Monday and arrange a meeting. I'll find a way to—"

"Not Monday," Yamaguchi said. "Give it some time. Let her—" He stopped. The sentence finished itself.

*Let her cool down. Let her wounded pride find somewhere else to go. Let the business relationship re-establish itself as more important than what just happened.*

"I'm sorry," Haruki said again.

"Don't apologize," Yamaguchi said, with the gruffness of a man who wants to say something kind and doesn't know how. "You didn't do anything wrong." He paused. "Just—" Another pause. "We'll talk Monday."

The car arrived at the office building. They all got out. Yamaguchi went immediately toward the station, his phone already back at his ear.

Haruki stood on the pavement in the rain for a moment, looking at nothing in particular.

Kenji stood a few feet away, documentation folder under his arm, coat collar up, not sure whether to say goodnight or whether some other response was appropriate.

"Nishimura-san," Haruki said.

Kenji looked at him.

"Sorry about the evening." He said it quietly, to the rain rather than to Kenji. "That was probably uncomfortable for you."

"It was fine," Kenji said. "The questions about the account went well."

Something almost like a smile. "Good. That's good." He looked at the street. A taxi went past, its light on. "Do you—" He stopped. Started again. "I was going to find somewhere to have a drink. Are you—"

He seemed, Kenji thought, to be asking the question the way people ask questions when they are not certain they should be asking them.

"Yes," Kenji said. "All right."

### Chapter Seven: A Bar in Shinjuku

The bar Haruki chose was not the kind of bar associated with corporate entertainment. It was small, in a basement in Shinjuku, with wooden walls and low lighting and the particular sound of a jazz record played at a volume intended to allow conversation without requiring it. There were perhaps twelve seats, most of them taken by people who were alone or in pairs and who had the look of people who had chosen this particular place precisely because no one would ask them to be anything.

They sat at the end of the bar. The bartender, an older man with a silver mustache, acknowledged them with a nod and set down coasters.

Haruki ordered whiskey. Kenji ordered the same, because it seemed simpler than explaining that he didn't usually drink whiskey, and because Haruki had ordered it with the easy authority of someone who knew what he was ordering and Kenji did not want to disrupt the rhythm of the moment.

For a while they didn't speak. The jazz record played. Haruki looked at his glass. Kenji looked at the shelves behind the bar, the rows of bottles in their different colors, amber and brown and gold.

"You don't have to stay," Haruki said. "I wasn't—I just didn't want to go home yet."

"I'm all right," Kenji said.

Another silence. Comfortable, somehow, in a way that silences with people one does not know are often not.

Haruki drank. Kenji watched him peripherally, the way one watches something one is not sure one should be watching.

"Is it always like that?" Kenji said, finally.

Haruki looked at him. "What?"

"People—" Kenji considered how to phrase it. "People wanting things from you. That you can't give them."

It was more direct than he usually was. He wasn't sure what had made him say it. Perhaps the whiskey, though he had barely touched it. Perhaps simply the quality of the moment — the bar, the rain audible even in the basement, Haruki's particular loosened-at-the-edges look, the way people who are usually composed look after a long difficult evening.

Haruki was quiet for a moment. Then he said: "More often than you'd think."

"That must be—" Kenji stopped.

"Exhausting?" Haruki smiled, but it was a different kind of smile from the ones he had worn at the party. Smaller. More honest. "Sometimes. I'm not—" He paused. "I'm not complaining. I know how that sounds. *Poor me, everyone likes me too much.*"

"I didn't think that," Kenji said.

"No?" Haruki looked at him with the directness that was apparently his default. "What did you think?"

Kenji considered this. "I thought it probably feels lonely sometimes. When people want a version of you rather than—" He stopped again, feeling he was going too far into the interior of something.

But Haruki was looking at him with an expression he couldn't quite identify — surprise, perhaps, the way people look surprised when something has come closer to the truth than they expected.

"Yes," he said. "That's—yes."

He poured another measure from the decanter the bartender had left. Kenji looked at his own glass and decided to try the whiskey, which burned pleasantly in his chest and made the low light seem warmer.

"Yamaguchi-san is going to be angry Monday," Haruki said, to the glass.

"He said you didn't do anything wrong."

"He said it." A pause. "He also looked at me like—" Haruki made a gesture with one hand that expressed something he couldn't articulate. "I've given him results every quarter for five years. And it still only takes one unhappy client to make all of that—" Another gesture. "Paper."

"It was her choice," Kenji said. "To be unhappy."

Haruki looked at him.

"She asked for something that wasn't appropriate and you declined, and she decided to turn that into a professional problem," Kenji said, with more firmness than he usually brought to opinions. "That's her character, not yours."

A moment of silence.

"You're very direct," Haruki said, and he sounded, Kenji thought, genuinely struck by this.

"I'm sorry."

"Don't be." Haruki looked at him for another moment. "It's—I don't hear that very often. People telling me what they actually think."

Kenji thought: *That's probably true. It's hard to be honest with people who are very beautiful and very successful. You're always aware of the imbalance.*

He didn't say this. He drank his whiskey instead and looked at the jazz musician on the album cover framed above the bar.

"Can I ask you something?" Haruki said.

"Of course."

"Why did you say yes tonight? Coming here. You don't know me."

Kenji thought about this. "You looked like you needed company," he said, simply. "And I—" He considered the second half of the sentence. "I didn't have anywhere else to be."

It was more honest than it was elegant, and he was aware of this. But Haruki smiled at it — the small, genuine smile, not the party smile — and something in the set of his shoulders released, very slightly, like a person finally setting down something they've been carrying all day.

"Thank you," he said. "For this."

"It's just a bar," Kenji said.

"Yes," Haruki said. "But company matters."

They sat in the small bar in Shinjuku, in the basement with the rain outside and the jazz record and the amber whiskey, for another hour. They talked — about nothing consequential, mostly: a book Kenji was reading, a particular client Haruki had once encountered who had insisted on testing every pen in the sample kit and had taken forty minutes to do so and had then ordered one box of ballpoints, a neighborhood in Tokyo they had both lived in at different times, whether the particular plant on Kenji's desk — Haruki had noticed it, apparently, in passing on the third floor, this small fact lodged itself in Kenji's mind without his entirely knowing why — was difficult to care for.

It was easy, in the way conversations are sometimes easy with people you don't know well enough to be guarded with, before the social machinery establishes itself and you begin managing impressions.

Walking to the station afterward, in the light rain, Haruki turned to him and said: "Next week — if you wanted to get lunch sometime. I eat alone most days, which I know sounds—"

"I eat alone too," Kenji said.

"Then maybe," Haruki said. "If you wanted."

"Yes," Kenji said. "I'd like that."

They went their separate ways at the station entrance, Haruki toward one line and Kenji toward another, and Kenji stood on the platform waiting for his train with the documentation folder under his arm and the small warmth of the whiskey in his chest and something else — something lighter, less easily categorized — and tried, without great success, to determine exactly what it was.

### Chapter Eight: Eyes That Follow

Monday came with the gray practicality of all Mondays.

Haruki arrived at eight forty-five, as always. He set up his desk, read his email, drank his coffee. But when he came off the stairwell and through the glass doors into the third floor, he saw Kenji immediately — at his desk near the back, head bent over his screen, a bento box open beside him and a paperback novel propped against his coffee cup. ---

Tuesday.

Haruki was at the coffee machine in the break room when the door opened and Kenji came in, carrying his empty mug and looking slightly surprised to find anyone there.

"Sorry," he said, which was his reflex — Haruki was learning — for any occasion when he felt he might be intruding.

"Don't apologize," Haruki said, which was his reflex, apparently, for Kenji apologizing.

They made their respective drinks side by side at the machine in a silence that was not uncomfortable. Kenji added two sugars to his coffee with the focus of someone performing a task that required precision. Haruki drank his black and watched this process with a curiosity he did not examine.

"How's the Tenmei situation?" Kenji said, not looking up from his coffee.

Kenji looked up. Behind his glasses, his eyes had the particular directness that Haruki had noticed at the bar — the way he sometimes said things more clearly than his general quietness suggested he was capable of.

"You're good at what you do," he said, simply. "I've seen the account records. Your clients don't just stay — they grow. That's not just charm. That's—" he considered the word "—care. You actually care about what you're selling them and whether it's right for them."

A moment of quiet.

"That's," Haruki said, and stopped. Started again. "Thank you."

### Chapter Nine: What You Notice

By the third week of October, Haruki had had lunch with Kenji four times.

He was aware that this was something he was choosing to do. This was not the kind of awareness that carries judgment with it — he was not evaluating the choice, not asking himself why. But it was present, a small noted fact, the way you note that you have been taking the same route home every day for a week when you could vary it.

He was also aware, in the way of someone whose professional life requires precise attention to the behavior of others, that he had begun to notice Kenji across the office.

Not the fourth floor. The third. He found reasons to go to the third floor with a frequency that was, probably, slightly more than strictly necessary. He went to check on documentation personally when an email would have served. He went to deliver sample materials that could have been sent through interoffice mail. He went, on two occasions, for no reason he could have articulated to a skeptical questioner.

And on the third floor, regardless of where he looked first, his eyes found Kenji.

At his desk, bent over his screen. In the break room, eating his lunch alone and reading his Norwegian mystery. Crossing to the printer with that particular careful walk of someone who does not want to be in anyone's way. Talking quietly with Hayashi-san, nodding attentively. Standing at the window for a moment with a cup of coffee, looking at the gray October sky with an expression of — what? Peace, perhaps. The particular peace of someone who is comfortable with solitude but not defined by it.

He was, Haruki thought, watching him without entirely meaning to, the most genuinely himself person he had encountered in years. Not performed. Not constructed. Whatever Kenji was in a given moment was simply what he was.

The cardigan was back — it had turned cold, proper autumn cold, and Kenji had apparently decided it was cardigan weather. It was a different one from the one Haruki had noticed in passing on the third floor weeks ago — a pale gray one, this time, slightly too large in the shoulders in the way of someone who has bought a size up for comfort. He wore it with complete lack of self-consciousness. It was, objectively, not a fashionable garment.

Haruki had noticed it three separate times.

He told himself he was simply observant. It was a professional skill — noticing details, reading people accurately, tracking changes. He was good at it. He applied it to everything.

He told himself this, and on a Thursday afternoon, standing at the elevator on the third floor after dropping off a set of sample materials he could absolutely have sent through the mail, watched the doors close on Kenji crossing back to his desk with his characteristic measured quiet, and thought: *I'm looking for him.*

Not just noticing. *Looking.*

The elevator arrived. He got in and looked at the panel of floor buttons with the expression of someone who has just remembered something surprising that they cannot immediately account for.

On Friday, Mishima Daisuke noticed that Haruki had been to the third floor three times that week and mentioned it to Okabe Shiro, because he noticed everything about Haruki in the way of people who resent someone and have organized their resentment into a monitoring system.

### Chapter Ten: Something Shifts

It was the last Friday in October when Haruki understood.

Not gradually. All at once, the way understanding sometimes arrives — a compression of things already known that suddenly achieves weight and form, that goes from being scattered observations to being something you cannot unknow.

He was sitting at his desk at four o'clock, finishing the week's reports, when Kenji came to the fourth floor for the first time since Haruki had known him. He came to deliver a set of corrected invoice records to the accounts team, which was on the fourth floor's south side — nothing to do with the sales desks, no reason at all for him to come past Haruki's area of the floor.

But the most direct route from the elevator to accounts passed Haruki's desk, and Kenji walked it, holding his folder with both hands, eyes slightly down in the particular way he had of moving through spaces that felt unfamiliar, making himself small, taking up less room than he actually needed.

He didn't see Haruki until he was almost at his desk.

"Nishimura-san," Haruki said.

Kenji looked up, and the small startled moment — the slight blink, the quick recalibration — was followed immediately by the smile. Not a performance. Not a social function. Just — a face becoming more itself.

"Kato-san. I didn't know you sat here."

"This is where I always sit," Haruki said, which was true and also slightly odd as a response, and he was aware of this.

"I'm delivering something to accounts," Kenji said, holding up the folder as evidence, which was also slightly odd and suggested he felt, for some reason, that his presence needed to be accounted for.

"Of course," Haruki said.

"I'll—" Kenji gestured vaguely toward accounts.

"Right," Haruki said.

Kenji went. Haruki watched him go — the cardigan, the slightly careful walk, the way he thanked the accounts person with the same attentive courtesy he apparently gave to everyone regardless of their position — and felt it arrive, unannounced, with the implacable force of things that are simply true:

*I want to see him.*

Not abstractly. Specifically. This person — Nishimura Kenji, who was quiet and wore a cardigan that was slightly too large and had clean glasses and read Norwegian mystery novels at his desk and said, with complete simplicity, *that's care, you actually care about what you're selling them* — this specific person, Haruki wanted to be around.

Not the party smile. Not the Toda Sakura kind of wanting, which was about something else entirely, something that had nothing to do with him. This was different. This was the kind of wanting that is about a person rather than about what they represent.

He looked at his screen. The report was half-finished.

He put his hands on the keyboard and sat there for a moment without typing anything.

*When did this happen,* he thought, without quite answering himself.

---

At four-thirty, Kenji came back past his desk on the way to the elevator, folder now empty, walking with the slightly more relaxed bearing of someone whose task has been completed.

"Nishimura-san," Haruki said, before he had decided to say anything.

Kenji stopped. "Yes?"

A pause. "I was going to—" Kenji stopped. Started again, with the transparency that Haruki had come to recognize as simply his way. "I was going to go home and read, actually."

"Would you have dinner instead?" Haruki said. "With me."

The particular quality of the silence that followed was something Haruki noticed with the precision of a person who reads silences professionally.

"Dinner," Kenji said.

"Yes."

"Just—" Kenji seemed to be sorting through the sentence, looking for the right configuration of the words. "The two of us."

"Yes," Haruki said.

Kenji looked at him from behind his clean glasses for a moment — that direct, unhurried look, the look that never tried to be anything other than what it was.

"All right," he said. "Yes."

### Chapter Eleven: Friday Evening

They went to a small restaurant near the office that Haruki had eaten at alone several times and that he had never brought anyone to, though he could not have explained why this distinction felt significant.

It was a ramen place, which was not the kind of restaurant one chose to make an impression, which was perhaps the point. Low wooden tables, menus on the wall, steam rising from the open kitchen. The kind of warmth that is immediately physical — the warmth of food and enclosed space and not being outside in the October cold.

Kenji looked around with the observational attention he brought to new environments — noting things, Haruki had come to understand, not out of anxiety but out of genuine interest in where he was. He had the quality of a person who paid attention to things that other people glossed over — the texture of surfaces, the arrangement of objects, the way a space had been put together. It was part of his thoroughness, Haruki thought. He did not partition his attentiveness; he gave it to everything.

"I've passed this place," Kenji said, "but I've never been in."

"The tonkotsu is very good," Haruki said.

"Then I'll have that."

The ordering was simple. The food came quickly. They ate, for a while, in the uncomplicated way of people who are comfortable enough together to not need conversation as a constant signal of engagement.

"Can I ask you something?" Haruki said.

Kenji looked up. "Of course."

"Why are you on the third floor?" He meant this genuinely — not condescendingly, not as a version of *why aren't you aiming higher,* but as a real question. "You're clearly—" He paused. "You're careful and precise and you see things clearly. You could have gone into sales, probably. Or finance."

Kenji considered this without appearing to be offended by the question. "I like my work," he said. "I like the documentation, the records — there's a—" he found the word carefully "—satisfaction in it. When something is well-maintained. "I also—" Kenji set down his chopsticks for a moment, looking at the table in the considering way that meant he was about to say something more honest than comfortable. I want to do my work well and go home and read and—" He stopped. Looked slightly self-conscious. "I know that's not—"

"It's honest," Haruki said.

"People think it means you're not trying," Kenji said. "Not caring. But it's not that. I care very much about doing my work well. I just don't care about—" He made a gesture that encompassed something Haruki understood immediately: the whole apparatus of professional ambition, the performance, the positioning.

"I know," Haruki said.

Kenji looked at him. "Do you?"

Haruki was quiet for a moment. "I care about my work," he said, slowly, the way you speak when you are figuring something out in real time. "I genuinely do. I like — when a client gets something that actually fits what they need, when the relationship is real rather than transactional. I like that." A pause. "But the—everything else. The numbers and the rankings and the—" He stopped. "I'm very good at performing confidence. At making people feel like they're in the presence of someone certain." He looked at his bowl. Kenji said nothing. He was listening with the complete quality of attention Haruki had never gotten used to.

"At the party," Haruki said, "that night — I knew I was handling it the right way. With Toda-san. I knew. But the whole drive home I kept thinking—" He stopped again. "About whether I'd miscalculated. Whether being right was actually a mistake, professionally. Whether—"

"You were right," Kenji said. Simply.

"I know."

"Then that's enough," Kenji said.

Such a simple thing. Such an entirely simple thing to say. Haruki looked at him — at this quiet, slightly rumpled man with his clean glasses and his precise attentiveness, who said what he meant without decorating it, who had sat in the bar with him in the rain and said *it was her choice* with the calm certainty of someone who has thought about justice and knows what it looks like — and felt something happen in his chest that was not unlike the feeling at his desk when Kenji had smiled at him across the fourth floor.

Something warm and something slightly vertiginous simultaneously.

*Oh,* he thought. *There it is again.*

He looked at his food. He ate. He did not say anything, and after a moment the conversation moved on, lightly and easily, to the Norwegian mystery and whether the translation was good, and to a particular notebook in Miyamoto's new collection that Haruki thought would be perfect for writers, and to what Kenji planned to do over the weekend.

### Chapter Twelve: November

November arrived with a particular cold that thinned the air and made the city seem more itself — the neon sharper, the quiet streets quieter.

Haruki went to the third floor every day.

He was aware that this was not professional. He was aware that there was no defensible logistical reason for the frequency of his visits, and that anyone paying attention — and Mishima Daisuke was certainly paying attention — could calculate it. He went anyway, with the slightly reckless deliberateness of someone who has decided to acknowledge something they cannot unknow.

Kenji always looked up when he arrived. Always gave him the small, genuine smile. Always made space — for Haruki's presence, for whatever he wanted to talk about, for silence if that was what the visit called for.

He was also, Haruki noticed with increasing detail, very specific in his kindnesses. It was not a general warmth — the kind Haruki himself deployed, which he was honest enough to recognize as partly professional — but a precise attentiveness to particular people and what they specifically needed. He noticed when Hayashi-san was stressed and left a cup of tea on her desk. He remembered, weeks later, that the junior clerk Sasamoto preferred her documents printed in a larger font. He asked after people's families and their projects and their dogs with the focus of someone who had actually been listening the last time these things were mentioned.

He was also, though he was entirely unaware of this — and this was what made it unbearable, in the way that genuine things are unbearable, in the way of an emotion too large for its container — quietly extraordinary. Not in a way the world had organized itself to recognize. In a way that required paying attention.

One Thursday, Haruki arrived on the third floor at lunchtime to find Kenji on the phone, speaking to what sounded like a supplier, resolving a discrepancy in an order with the patient clarity of someone who has been through this particular kind of problem before and knows exactly how to find the path through it.

On the phone, Kenji was different and the same. His voice had a quiet authority that was not present in social situations — the authority of genuine expertise, of a person who knows exactly what they're talking about and doesn't need to perform certainty because they have it. He worked through the discrepancy methodically, referencing specific dates and order numbers from memory, suggesting a resolution with the natural ease of someone who has already done the work of understanding the problem before speaking.

"Sorry," he said. "That took longer than expected."

"Don't apologize," Haruki said.

"You heard all of that?"

A pause. The particular color of Kenji's expression — not embarrassed, exactly, but slightly caught, the way people look when a compliment lands somewhere real.

"Thank you," he said.

"You said that to me once," Haruki said.

"I know."

"It's different, hearing it."

"Yes," Kenji said. "It is."

They looked at each other for a moment, with the particular quality of two people who are both aware that a conversation has arrived, unexpectedly, at something more honest than either was prepared for.
