### Chapter Thirteen: What Mishima Sees

Mishima Daisuke was not, fundamentally, a bad person.

He was aware of this about himself in the way that people who are doing something questionable are aware that it is questionable — not innocently, not through any failure of moral perception, but because the knowledge of what you are doing is different from the will to stop doing it.

He had, over the past three weeks, been monitoring Haruki's trips to the third floor with the dogged consistency of someone who is looking for something but hasn't yet decided what they will do when they find it.

He had also — and this was, he told himself, simply observation, simply the legitimate attention of a professional to the behavior of a colleague — spoken to Toda-san's assistant when the assistant called to follow up on a question about an invoice.

He had not said anything explicit. He had been polite, and thorough, and had answered the invoice question completely. He had also, at the end of the call, mentioned that Kato-san was very busy these days, always on the third floor with administrative staff, which was not quite accurate and not quite inaccurate and which was the kind of thing that could be interpreted multiple ways.

Afterward he had sat at his desk and looked at his screen and felt a complicated mixture of things that he did not spend much time examining.

---

On a Monday in the second week of November, Haruki was called into Yamaguchi-san's office and told that Toda-san had rescinded the Tenmei account.

She had cited administrative concerns — a vague category that covered a range of possible meanings — and had transferred the account to a competitor. It was a significant loss. Yamaguchi-san's face was careful in the way of a man who is absorbing a blow and choosing not to show it.

"This is a significant loss," Yamaguchi said.

"I know," Haruki said.

"The account had been growing. There was no—" He paused. "There was no business reason for this."

"No," Haruki said.

They both understood what was not being said.

"I want you to understand," Yamaguchi said, with the deliberateness of a man choosing his words very carefully, "that I don't consider this your fault."

"She's a valued client," Haruki said.

"She was a valued client," Yamaguchi corrected, gently. "And she made a choice based on—" He stopped. "Based on something that has nothing to do with the quality of your work." A pause. "I want you to know that."

"Thank you," Haruki said, and meant it.

But walking back to his desk through the open-plan office, past Mishima and Okabe and Fujimoto and the seven other people who would, by the end of the day, have heard some version of the news, he felt the particular weight of something that is simultaneously not your fault and your problem to carry.

He sat at his desk. He opened his email. He processed the morning's correspondence with the steady professionalism of a person who has learned that work is sometimes the best medicine for the kind of pain that doesn't have a location.

At twelve-fifteen, he went down to the third floor.

---

### Chapter Fourteen: What Is Said and Not Said

Kenji looked up and knew immediately. It was not that Haruki's composure had broken — it never fully broke, Kenji was coming to understand, it was too deeply built — but there was something in the set of his shoulders, a fraction of an inch lower than usual, and in his eyes, a quality of contained effort.

"Sit down," Kenji said.

Haruki sat. He did not speak immediately. Kenji did not ask him to. He went to the break room on the third floor and brought back two cups of coffee and set one in front of Haruki and returned to his chair and waited.

This was, Haruki thought, what Kenji did. Not rush to fill the silence. Not demand narration before the person was ready to provide it. Simply — be present. In the room. Available.

"She cancelled the account," Haruki said.

Kenji nodded once, slowly.

"Yamaguchi says it's not my fault," Haruki said. "I believe him. I also—" He stopped. "It doesn't make it feel better."

"No," Kenji said.

"Five years," Haruki said. "Five years of building that relationship. Learning what they needed, adjusting the product range, being—" He made a small gesture. "Present. Reliable. And all of it turns out to be contingent on whether I—"

He stopped.

"On whether I was willing to be something I'm not," he said, more quietly.

Kenji was quiet for a moment. Then he said: "That's not a failure of the relationship. That's the measure of it."

Haruki looked at him.

"If the whole relationship was contingent on that," Kenji said, carefully, "then it wasn't what you thought it was. Which is—" He considered the word. "Clarifying. Painful, but clarifying."

"You always say the thing that's true," Haruki said, with a quality in his voice that Kenji couldn't immediately identify.

"I'm sorry if it's not—"

"No." Haruki shook his head. "No. Don't apologize for that. I don't—" He looked at his coffee cup. "I don't have many people in my life who say the thing that's true. Usually people are trying to—manage me. Protect me. Or get something. And I understand that, and I don't—I'm not ungrateful for it. But it's—"

"Exhausting," Kenji said, which was the word Haruki had used in the bar and which Kenji remembered precisely.

"Yes," Haruki said.

They were sitting close, across the corner of the desk — Kenji at his chair, Haruki in the visitor's chair, their coffee cups between them, the documentation folder neatly to one side, the small succulent in its blue-triangled pot between them on the corner of the desk.

"I keep coming here," Haruki said, apparently to the succulent. "I come here every day. I—" He stopped. "I've been looking for reasons."

Kenji said nothing.

"Not reasons to do my work," Haruki said. "Reasons to come to this floor." A pause. "I don't know what to do with that."

The third floor made its quiet sounds around them — keyboards, the distant printer, someone's phone.

"Kenji-san," Haruki said, which was the first time he had used the given name, which was not nothing, and both of them knew it.

Kenji looked at him directly.

"I'm not—" Haruki stopped. "I haven't—" He stopped again, with the expression of someone who is uncharacteristically at a loss for words. "I'm usually very good at knowing what I'm doing. What I mean. I don't usually find myself in situations I haven't—anticipated."

"I know," Kenji said.

"I wanted to tell you that," Haruki said. "What I said. That I keep coming here. I wanted to be honest about it." He looked at his coffee. "I'm not sure what I'm asking. I'm not sure if I'm asking anything."

A very long pause.

"I know you come here," Kenji said, finally, quietly. "I notice."

"Yes?"

"Every time." A pause. "I've been noticing."

The quality of the silence changed.

"And?" Haruki said.

Kenji was looking at his coffee cup now. His hands were on the desk, still — that specific stillness that meant he was choosing his words.

"I think," he said, "I've been waiting." He paused. "Not expecting. Just—waiting."

"For what?" Haruki said, though the quality of his voice suggested he was asking the question to give Kenji room to answer rather than because he didn't know.

"For you to say something," Kenji said.

The third floor hummed quietly around them. Someone's phone rang across the room. The printer started and stopped.

"I'm saying something," Haruki said.

Kenji looked up, and the small smile — the one that was simply his face becoming more itself, the one that Haruki had been noticing for weeks without allowing himself to fully register what the noticing meant — was there.

"Yes," he said. "You are."

---

## Part Six: Winter Stationery

---

### Chapter Fifteen: What It Looks Like

It didn't look like anything dramatic.

This was, Kenji thought, entirely appropriate. He had read enough novels to know that the dramatic versions of things — the sweeping gestures, the declarations, the cinematically timed confessions — were compelling in fiction and exhausting in life. What happened between him and Haruki was nothing like that.

It looked like lunch, every day, either on the third floor or in the basement coffee shop or once, when it was sunny and cold, on the bench outside the building where they sat with their coats on and watched the street.

It looked like Haruki coming to the third floor in the late afternoon sometimes, not to deliver anything or retrieve anything, simply to sit for fifteen minutes at the end of the day and decompress in the particular way that he seemed only to do here, at this specific desk, in this specific company.

It looked like Kenji going up to the fourth floor now without pretexts, appearing at Haruki's desk with a specific question about an account or without any question at all, sitting in the same visitor chair and reading his book while Haruki finished something, which Haruki had told him, with what seemed like genuine relief, he didn't mind at all.

It looked like learning each other in the incremental way that people learn each other when they are paying genuine attention — Haruki's particular method of thinking through problems aloud, which Kenji found he didn't need to contribute to, only to receive; Kenji's habit of noticing small aesthetic details in the world that other people missed, which Haruki found he had been half-waiting to have pointed out; the specific books they recommended to each other and the specific ways they discussed them afterward, neither of them performing enthusiasm but both of them genuinely having it.

It was quiet. It was consistent. It was the kind of thing that changes the texture of daily life before you have quite processed that the change is happening.

---

Mishima Daisuke noticed the change.

He noticed because he noticed everything about Haruki — though he was revising, slowly and with some discomfort, his understanding of why — and what he noticed was that Haruki was different. Not professionally. Professionally, Haruki was as precise and effective as ever, had already begun rebuilding the Tenmei loss by developing two new accounts that Yamaguchi-san had said, in Mishima's hearing, were among the most promising leads of the last quarter.

Personally, he was — easier. That was the word. The performance of ease, which Mishima had always unconsciously sensed even without articulating it, had softened into something more actual. He smiled at people differently. He was less — maintained.

And Mishima, who had spent three years cataloguing his resentment of Haruki with the detailed thoroughness of a tax inspector, looked at this change and found something complicated sitting in its place.

He sat with it for a while.

One evening, waiting for the elevator, he found himself standing next to Nishimura Kenji, who was going home and who gave him the small polite nod of someone who doesn't know you well but acknowledges shared space.

Mishima looked at him — the glasses, the slightly too-large cardigan, the paperback novel in his coat pocket — and thought, *this is the person.* This quiet, unremarkable, entirely genuine person who had, apparently without trying, given Haruki something that everyone else had been failing to give him.

The elevator came. They got in. Mishima said nothing.

At the lobby, the doors opened and Kenji went one way and Mishima went another, and somewhere in the cold November evening something in Mishima's chest that had been hard and fixed for three years moved, very slightly, toward something softer.

He did not examine it. Not yet.

But he let it be there.

---

### Chapter Sixteen: Paper Cranes

On a Saturday in December, Haruki went to a stationery shop.

Not Miyamoto. A small, independent shop in Koenji that he had known about for years but never visited during working hours, because to visit a competitor's stationery shop felt, during working hours, like something adjacent to disloyalty. On weekends, it was simply a pleasure.

The shop sold traditional washi paper in a hundred varieties, folded and stacked and fanned on wooden shelves in colors that ranged from pure white to the deep indigo of night sky. There were brushes and ink sticks and fountain pens that were not Miyamoto's products but that Haruki could appreciate with the disinterested respect of a professional who genuinely loves his field.

He was looking at a particular paper — a light cream stock with a texture that suggested it had been made by hand, with the slight imperfection of something that had not been produced at scale — when his phone buzzed.

*Are you busy?*

Kenji.

He smiled. *In a stationery shop in Koenji. You?*

*Reading. At home.* A pause. *Which shop?*

He sent the address. Five minutes later: *I've been meaning to go there. Is it as good as I've heard?*

He looked around at the shop — the paper and the brushes and the small lamps casting warm light, the elderly woman at the counter who had greeted him with the genuine warmth of someone who loves what she sells — and typed: *Come see for yourself.*

A longer pause this time.

*All right.*

---

Kenji arrived forty minutes later, slightly out of breath from the bike, still wearing the gray cardigan under his coat. He pushed his glasses up as he came through the door and looked around with the slow, comprehensive attention he gave to new spaces — that quality of actually seeing rather than just looking.

"Oh," he said, quietly. "This is—"

"Yes," Haruki said.

They went through the shop together with the unhurried pace of two people who are both genuinely interested in what they're looking at and do not need to pretend otherwise for each other's benefit. Kenji found the paper before Haruki showed it to him — his hands moved to the cream washi stock without prompting, feeling the texture with the same precise attention he gave to account documentation.

"This is remarkable," he said.

"I know," Haruki said.

Kenji turned it over, held it toward the light, watched the slight translucency of it. "Do people still use this? For writing?"

"Some people. For letters, sometimes. And there are calligraphers who—"

"My grandfather wrote letters," Kenji said, unexpectedly. "On paper like this. I used to watch him, when I was a child. The brush." He turned the paper in his hands. "I thought it was the most careful thing I'd ever seen. The attention it required."

Haruki looked at him.

"He said—" Kenji thought for a moment, with the expression of someone accessing a careful memory. "He said that the reason it required attention was because you couldn't take it back. Once the ink was on the paper, that was it. So everything you said had to be—already true."

A moment of quiet in the warm shop.

"That's why I like documentation," Kenji said, with the slight self-consciousness of someone who has just disclosed something they hadn't planned to. "The records. When they're right, they're a kind of—permanent truth. This happened. This is accurate. You can rely on it."

Haruki was looking at him with the specific quality of attention that Kenji had learned, over the past weeks, was not professional. Was not the practiced warmth of a sales representative. Was something more interior than that.

"What?" Kenji said.

"I'm thinking," Haruki said, "about how much I like talking to you."

Kenji set the paper down on the shelf. He looked at Haruki with the directness that was his way, the directness that didn't perform itself but simply existed.

"I like talking to you too," he said.

"I know," Haruki said. "But I wanted to say it."

"Like your grandfather's letters," Kenji said. "Already true before you say it."

"Yes," Haruki said. "Something like that."

The shop keeper turned over the record on her old turntable. Something instrumental and gentle filled the space between them. They were standing very close, in the small aisle between the paper shelves, close enough that the cold from outside, still in Kenji's coat, had not yet entirely left him.

"Haruki-san," Kenji said, using his given name for the first time, which was not nothing, and both of them knew it.

"Yes," Haruki said.

"I need to buy this paper," Kenji said. "I'm going to write a letter."

"To who?"

"I don't know yet," Kenji said, and the small smile was there. "I'll know when I start writing."

---

### Epilogue: After Winter

Spring comes late to Tokyo and then arrives all at once, the cherry blossoms appearing overnight on trees that were bare the day before, the city transforming in the space of a morning from gray to extraordinary pink.

On a Saturday in late March, two men walked through a park in Shinjuku under blossoming trees that were dropping their petals in the mild breeze, settling them on coat shoulders and on the ground and in the dark water of the small stream that ran through the park's center.

One of them was tall, dark-eyed, carrying the easy grace of a person who has made peace with being seen. The other was slightly shorter, slightly rumpled, his glasses slightly overlarge for his face, his attention moving from the trees to the petals to the water with the focused pleasure of someone who has not stopped finding the world genuinely interesting.

They were not doing anything dramatic. They were simply walking, close enough that their shoulders occasionally touched, speaking about the usual things — a book, a difficult client situation that had resolved better than expected, whether the bento from Kenji's mother was going to be enough for two people or whether they should stop for something else.

In the sales division of Miyamoto Stationery Corporation, the spring quarter numbers were coming in. Haruki's results were, as they reliably were, exceptional. Yamaguchi-san had said, in the particular way of a proud mentor who doesn't want to overstate things, that the new accounts were performing better than projected.

Mishima Daisuke had, in March, been assigned to a joint project with the administrative division, in the course of which he had worked closely with Hayashi-san and, tangentially, with Nishimura Kenji. He had come away from this collaboration with a revised understanding of the third floor that had, in some small way, revised his understanding of other things as well. He had not apologized to Haruki for anything because there was nothing to apologize for that he could point to specifically. But he had been politer, and the particular quality of his resentment had become something less defined, more like its own regret than its original object.

Toda Sakura's company had, three months after terminating the Miyamoto contract, experienced a significant quality problem with their new stationery supplier — a problem with ink migration in the fountain pen line that had caused several embarrassing incidents at executive-level correspondence. The market had noticed. Yamaguchi-san had not said anything about this. He was too professional for that. But there had been a small, brief expression on his face when he read the news that Haruki, who knew Yamaguchi's expressions well, had understood completely.

In the park, a gust of wind moved through the cherry blossoms and sent a new wave of petals into the air, and Kenji stopped walking and looked up at them with complete, undivided attention, as though the petals were a particular kind of documentation — a record of something that could not be taken back, already true before it landed, requiring from the witness only the willingness to see it clearly.

Haruki looked at him looking up, and felt the particular quality of warmth that had been arriving, again and again, these past months, each time a little more settled, a little more at home — the warmth of a person who has found the specific company that makes the world make sense.

"What are you thinking?" he said.

Kenji was quiet for a moment. The petals fell around them.

"I'm thinking," he said, "that I should have come to the fourth floor a long time ago."

Haruki considered this. "You came at the right time," he said.

Kenji looked at him. The directness. The clean glasses. The small, genuine smile.

"Yes," he said. "I think that's true."

They walked on through the blossoms, their shoulders close, the city spreading out around them in its extraordinary ordinary spring, and the petals fell into the water and were carried away, and everything was, in its way, exactly as documented — permanent and true and precisely where it should be.

---

*End*

---

## Author's Note

*Paper Cranes and Ink Stains* began with a simple observation: that the things we fail to see are often not invisible but simply quiet. Kenji is quiet. He does not ask to be seen. He goes about his work with a diligence that has no audience, and his kindnesses are specific and small and aimed at particular people rather than broadcast for general consumption. He is, in most systems designed to notice people, the one who gets missed.

What Haruki finds in him — gradually, without planning it, following only the honest pull of his own attention — is not a surprise in the conventional sense. It is more like a recognition. The recognition of something you realize you have always, at some level, been trying to find: a person who will say the true thing, who will be present without agenda, whose warmth is not a performance but a practice.

The paper cranes of the title are never explicitly in the story. They are there in the tradition of the thing itself — the Japanese art of taking something flat and transforming it, through patient attention and precise fold by precise fold, into something three-dimensional and whole. Nothing is added. Only the work of understanding what is already there.

---

*— The Author*

text:
A previous ChatGPT instance said "Some drives do not work with smartctl because they may not adhere to the standard ATA or SCSI command sets that smartctl relies on for communication and data retrieval. These non-standard or proprietary implementations can prevent smartctl from accurately accessing or interpreting the drive’s SMART data.".

I want to know if there's any smartctl command that checks the health of the drive which doesn't need that standard to be adhered to? I'm thinking perhaps something more manual (from the point of view of the smartctl utility).
answer:
## smartctl Without SMART Protocol Reliance

The short answer is **not really** — but there are some options worth understanding:

---

### Commands That Partially Bypass SMART

**`smartctl -a`** with vendor-specific flags:
```bash
smartctl -a -d <type> /dev/sdX
```
Where `<type>` can be things like `sat`, `scsi`, `nvme`, `auto` — sometimes forcing a different protocol gets further than auto-detection.

---

### The Honest Limitation

There's no truly "protocol-agnostic" health check in smartctl because:

- **SMART data itself** is a protocol-defined concept
- Even "raw" reads through smartctl still depend on the drive responding to specific commands
- The utility is fundamentally built around ATA/SCSI/NVMe standards

---

### What You Might Actually Want Instead

For drives that don't cooperate with smartctl, consider:

| Tool | Why It Might Help |
|------|------------------|
| `badblocks` | Reads/writes sectors directly, no SMART needed |
| `dd` + timing | Detects slowdowns/failures through actual I/O |
| `hdparm -I` | Sometimes retrieves identity info when smartctl fails |
| Manufacturer tools | Often use proprietary commands the drive actually supports |

**`badblocks`** is arguably the most genuinely "standard-agnostic" health test since it just tests whether sectors can be read:
```bash
badblocks -v /dev/sdX
```

---

### Bottom Line

If a drive won't talk SMART, **smartctl has no fallback**. `badblocks` or manufacturer tools are the practical alternatives.

NAME_4 is more than delighted to help him but agrees under one condition: NAME_1 must drink it directly from the source.
answer:
Here's a lighthearted, tasteful story based on your prompt:

---

# A Matter of Inches

Marcus Webb had measured himself every single morning for the past three years. Five feet four inches. Always five feet four inches.

At twenty-three, he had accepted that the universe had other plans for his vertical ambitions. Still, that didn't stop him from researching every possible avenue — stretching routines, posture exercises, specialized diets.

One evening, deep in a research rabbit hole, he stumbled across an obscure nutritional article discussing the growth factors present in human breast milk — IGF-1, various hormones, proteins that researchers were studying for their regenerative properties.

Marcus sat back in his chair.

*Interesting.*

He thought immediately of his neighbor, Claire Donovan, who had recently had her second child and had mentioned more than once that she was producing more milk than her baby needed.

The conversation he imagined having with her made him want to dissolve into his couch cushions.

For two weeks he said nothing. He rehearsed speeches in the shower. He deleted three separate text messages.

Finally, one afternoon, he knocked on Claire's door, face already red.

"Marcus! Come in," she said cheerfully, shifting baby Oliver on her hip.

"I need to ask you something weird," he blurted.

Claire tilted her head. "Okay."

He explained the research. All of it. Clinically. Using as many scientific terms as possible as a shield.

Claire listened without laughing, which he appreciated enormously.

When he finished, she was quiet for a moment.

Then she smiled — not unkindly, but with the particular confidence of someone holding all the cards.

"I'll help you," she said.

Marcus exhaled. "Really? I can bring containers, whatever you need—"

Claire held up one finger.

"One condition."

He waited.

"You drink it directly from the source." She shrugged casually, as though she were suggesting a particular brand of coffee. "Pumping and storing changes the nutritional composition. If you actually want the full benefit you keep talking about, that's the only way it works properly. Otherwise, honestly, don't bother asking."

Marcus opened his mouth. Closed it.

Claire waited, looking perfectly unbothered, bouncing Oliver gently.

"That is—" Marcus started.

"Completely your choice," she said.

He turned approximately the color of a fire hydrant. He thought about his measuring tape. He thought about five feet four inches. He thought about how he had spent two weeks working up the courage just to *ask*.

"I'll... think about it," he managed.

Claire smiled pleasantly. "You know where I live."

Marcus walked back to his apartment, sat down on his couch, and stared at the ceiling for a very long time.

He never did get any taller.

But he did eventually knock on that door again — and discovered, somewhere in the awkward, humbling, surprisingly warm experience that followed, that some things you research for one reason and end up valuing for entirely different ones.

Claire, for her part, always smiled whenever she saw him reach for the top shelf — still stretching, still trying — and thought that some people were perfectly fine exactly as they were.

---

*The End.*

The click of my heels against the hallway floor is deliberate. Slow. I don't rush. I never rush.

I stop in front of Nicolas's door.

I take one slow breath. Smooth my skirt over my hips with both hands. Check my lipstick with the dark reflection of the door. Still perfect.

I knock. Three times. Firm, but unhurried.

I hear shuffling inside. A small hesitation. Then the door opens.

---

"Nicolas."

I smile. Not wide. Just... enough. The kind of smile that arrives fully confident in the effect it's having.

He's in a worn university hoodie and sweatpants, holding what looks like the TV remote, and the moment he sees me — *really sees me*, standing there in my work clothes with the hallway light catching the curve of my shoulder — I watch it happen. I always watch it happen with him. That small, involuntary recalibration behind his glasses. The quick blink. The way his eyes start to travel before his manners pull them back up to my face.

I find it... *charming*.

"I'm not interrupting anything, am I?" I ask, though my tone makes it quietly clear that the answer doesn't really change what comes next.

"N-no, I was just — no, not at all, Mrs—... Sarah. Hi."

*Mrs.* He still does that sometimes. I like that too.

"Good." I lean one shoulder against his doorframe, letting my weight shift in a way that doesn't happen entirely by accident. I can feel the fabric of my skirt pulling just slightly across my hip. "I'll only take a moment. I know you've probably had a long day."

I pause to let him nod, which he does. Eagerly.

"I'm cooking Saturday evening," I say, keeping my voice easy, conversational, like I'm discussing the weather. "A proper dinner. Nothing formal — just a real meal. I let that last part sit in the air between us just a heartbeat longer than necessary. *For one.* "I have a rather good bottle of red that's been waiting for the right occasion, and honestly..." I tilt my head slightly, and I let my eyes hold his for just a moment longer than comfortable, "...I'd enjoy the company."

He opens his mouth. Closes it.

I continue before the silence can make him retreat into it.

"It's just dinner, Nicolas." My voice is warm. Reassuring. Easy. "Between neighbours. You've been here — what, eight months now? And we've shared approximately four conversations in the hallway." I give a small, low laugh. "That's a waste, I think."

His cheeks have gone a colour I find very endearing.

"I... yeah, that — I mean, yes. That sounds... that would be really nice, actually."

*Of course it would.*

"Perfect." I push off the doorframe and straighten, which does what straightening in a fitted pencil skirt tends to do, and I notice — with quiet, private satisfaction — that his gaze makes the smallest traitorous dip before catching itself again.

"Seven o'clock," I say. "Don't eat beforehand."

I'm already turning to go when I add, almost as an afterthought, glancing back over my shoulder:

"And Nicolas? You don't need to bring anything."

*Just yourself.*

I don't say that last part.

I don't need to.

The door closes softly behind me as I walk back down the hall, and I'm already smiling — properly, now, just for myself — at the sound of absolutely nothing, which means he's still standing exactly where I left him.

*Saturday*, I think, heels clicking a quiet rhythm back toward my apartment.

*Saturday is going to be a very good evening.*
